newsitem.title: UK: Prostestant clergyman urges N.Irish parades peace.
newsitem.headline: Prostestant clergyman urges N.Irish parades peace.

text.p: Achbishop Robin Eames, primate of the Protestant Church of Ireland, issued a fervent appeal for peace in Northern Ireland on Thursday as sectarian tension heightened in the run-up to a hotly disputed pro-British street parade.
"Northern Ireland cannot be allowed to face a repetition of the event of last summer," said the clergyman, whose congregation in the Anglican communion church lives on both sides of the Irish border.

He was echoing widespread anxiety that a proposed Protestant Orange Order parade and a Roman Catholic counter-demonstration on Sunday in the town of Portadown might trigger more chaos this year after ugly scenes in the town last year.

Speaking before prime ministersTony Blair of Britain and Bertie Ahern of Ireland met in London for talks about the parade and the stalled peace process in the British province, Eames warned that fringe elements bent on violence could manipulate public demonstrations.

"That danger is ever present and must not be forgotten," he said in a statement. "In God's name let none of us by word or action condemn Northern Ireland to a period of further violence, suffering and division."

In London, a senior British official said Blair and Ahern held a "friendly, constructive and positive" 90-minute meeting during which the Irish premier expressed general support for Britain's approach to the peace process.
"There was a clear, shared determination to try to keep the peace process on track," the official said.

Ahern and Foreign Minister Ray Burke, who came to power in a coalition government last week, made it clear during a rare visit north to Belfast on Tuesday that they would oppose any move by Britain to use force against Catholic protesters to ensure the march goes through.
The official said Ahern and Burke, who also attended Thursday's talks in London, did not restate their position and said they appreciated the difficulties facing Britain over the Portadown parade.
"Nobody is in any doubt it's a very difficult situation," he said, adding a decision would be taken soon whether to allow the march to go ahead.

Controversy about the Portadown parade, coming in the runup to the climax of a traditionally turbulent "marching season" by the Protestant Order, has added to instability caused by resurgent IRA guerrillas who are fighting to end British rule.

George Mitchell, a former U.S. senator and chairman of slow-moving multi-party peace negotiations, said a repetition of last year's violence would "have an adverse effect on the attitudes and atmosphere at the talks".
He told BBC radio that if the season passed off peacefully, that would "have a beneficial and encouraging effect".

Britain banned the parade last year but reversed the decision when Protestant hardliners forced the province to a virtual halt during four days of riots and road blockades. Catholic gangs then went on a rampage against he police.
Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam condemned as outrageous an outlawed Protestant guerrilla group's threat to kill Irish Catholics if London bows to Dublin pressure against the parade.
Britain and Ireland are worried that spillover violence will harden attitudes and slow down efforts to achieve a political settlement and secure an end to Irish Republican Army violence.
The Orange Order holds hundreds of marches across the province culminating on July 12 which is the anniversary of old battlefield triumphs over the Catholic Irish.
Mowlam told BBC radio that intense efforts had not yet achieved an agreement between the Order and the Catholics.
"One has to try to get an accommodation, because if not then violence is most likely," she told BBC radio.
